newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive-Real power with Cabinet.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive-Real power with Cabinet.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Dec 17 - New ministers in the Bolger-Peters coalition government started earning their $126,000-plus salaries yesterday after taking their oaths of office at Government House.

A formal Cabinet meeting initiated the rookie ministers, six of them in the inner Cabinet, and six outside, into the rituals of executive procedure, as well as initiating work on the budget policy statement.

The first business session of Cabinet is set down for Wednesday, and is likely to have a full agenda, given the issues shuffled into the "pending" basket by the caretaker administration during the eight weeks of coalition talks.

Already the new government has a fair bit of catch-up, for example, on the budget policy statement due out in February, which is expected to define more clearly the fiscal policy of the National-NZ First coalition.

And Cabinet as its first step to initiating the work programme of the coalition agreement signed last week may issue instructions to law drafting officials to prepare bills required early in 1997 to delay the July tax cuts, and to abolish the superannuation surcharge (which is to come into effect on April 1 1998).

New Treasurer Winston Peters, who assumes responsibility for monetary and fiscal policy, may also push for legislation to amend the Fiscal Responsibility Act and the Reserve Bank Act to allow him to exercise the authority currently vested in the Minister of Finance.
These changes are important to the NZ First leader, since they signal the significance of his role at that expense of National's Bill Birch.
According to Peters, the division of duties between the Treasurer and the Finance Minister follows the Australian model. He says that setting tax policy will be part of the function of Treasurer.
But constitutional experts point out that in the New Zealand system policy issues are thrashed out in the Cabinet committee structure and finally in the full Cabinet.
Past administrations have included a Cabinet expenditure and revenue control committee which has the function of approving funds for business-as-usual activities.
A gatekeeping committee reviews new initiatives and then sets priorities.
The conclusions of these committee are then passed on the Cabinet Strategy Committee, and then move on to the full Cabinet.
The coalition agreement acknowledges that some of the policies agreed by the parties will call for additional spending not anticipated in the 1996 budget.
To that extent National and NZ First agreed that a budgetary programme prioritising expenditure will be prepared "with the consent of both parties".

This indicates that work on the priorities will clearly be assigned to the appropriate Cabinet committees, and the papers prepared by officials will go to both the Treasurer and the Minister of Finance.
And since the Cabinet Strategy Committee has customarily been chaired by the Prime Minister, the agenda is in effect controlled by him.

The coalition agreement stipulates that agendas are drawn up by the Cabinet Office and submitted for approval to the Prime Minister "in consultation with the other coalition party leader in advance of Cabinet meetings".

It adds that as a general rule Cabinet papers are to be considered by Cabinet committees before reference to Cabinet "and as a general rule, Cabinet papers are required to have been through formal consultation procedures among the Coalition partners before being placed on the agenda".
Cabinet papers are to be distributed to all ministers of Cabinet.

While the Treasurer will be the channel through which the government's instructions will be passed to Treasury, and through which recommendations from Treasury are passed back to government, Birch as Minister of Finance will have access to all streams of advice from Treasury.
And, as the coalition agreement stipulates, competing points of view, if any, in Cabinet committees will be submitted to Cabinet.
So, if theoretically the Treasurer has the power for example to sack the Reserve Bank governor for failure to meet the inflation target, the real power rests with Cabinet.
